days.title: The Donor
days.scenario:
Elena is dying of liver failure. Her brother Marco is the only compatible living donor. He offers a lobe of his liver, which will save her life, but he sets one condition: she must first tell their elderly mother the truth about the fire that killed their father twenty years ago. Elena caused it, by accident, as a teenager. Marco took the blame to protect her, and their mother has grieved him as a reckless boy ever since.

Marco says he has carried the lie long enough, and that he cannot give his sister his body while she lets their mother die believing a falsehood about him. Elena says the truth would shatter their mother in her final years, and that Marco is using a scalpel to force a confession.

Without the surgery, Elena dies within months. With it, their mother learns what her daughter did.
days.question: Should Elena meet his condition?
days.option_a_text: She should tell the truth. Marco has a right not to give his own flesh while remaining a scapegoat, and their mother deserves to know her son.
days.option_b_text: She should refuse. A life-saving gift extracted by ultimatum is coercion, and sparing a frail old woman needless anguish is its own duty.

days.title: The Academy
days.scenario:
Marek is fifteen and has been offered a place at a football academy abroad. Training is full-time; the school attached to it stops at basic literacy. Roughly one boy in thirty from the academy signs a professional contract. The rest come home at nineteen with no qualifications.

His mother has the figures in front of her. She also has the letter Marek wrote her, in which he says that when he is on the pitch he stops thinking about his father's illness, and that this is the only place he has ever been good at something. He feels as if there are no other life prospects for him.

He has two years of school left. His teachers say he is capable, but unmotivated, and unlikely to leave with much. He is, however, an exceptional player. The academy will not hold the place open.

His father, who taught him to play in the yard, has perhaps a year left. He told Marek to go. He also told his wife, privately, that he wants to see one match before the end.
days.question: Should his mother let him go?
days.option_a_text: Let him go. He gets one chance at the thing that makes him whole, and he may resent her for denying him the opportunity.
days.option_b_text: Keep him in school. Twenty-nine out of thirty boys come home to nothing, and at fifteen he cannot consent to a future he can't yet imagine.

days.title: The Statement
days.scenario:
A woman is appointed to run the city's ambulance service, which has been failing for years. She is widely regarded as the only person capable of fixing it, and within a year response times have fallen sharply.

A journalist then uncovers a paper she wrote twelve years ago, at twenty-nine, already a qualified registrar, and presented to a health policy conference. In it she argued that the elderly poor consumed more healthcare than they contribute and should sit lower in the queue where the resource is finite. It was an argument made seriously that she presented with data. There is a recording. She has never publicly repeated the view, and has spent the years since in public medicine, much of it in geriatric care.

Eighteen months ago she designed a triage protocol that deprioritises repeat low-acuity callers from residential settings. An independent clinical body has reviewed it and called it sound. It is also the single change that most improved response times overall, and the group it moves down the queue is, in practice, the frail elderly. Nobody can say whether the reasoning behind it is the reasoning in the recording. 

She declines to say she has changed her mind. However, when pressed multiple, she eventually says she will not perform a recantation of her presentation if she cannot say it is sincere.

Since the recording surfaced, emergency calls from the city's over-seventies have fallen eleven percent. The clinical director believes some of those are people who should be calling and are not, but cannot say how many.

The council may dismiss her without cause. There are other competent successor options, but none directly comparable to her and her results.
days.question: Should she be removed from her post?
days.option_a_text: Yes. Public office rests on public trust, and no one who once argued that some lives are less deserving of medical attention can hold that much power.
days.option_b_text: No. She should be judged by years of work and positive results, not twelve-year-old words, and removing her punishes the patients she is actively saving.

days.title: The Second Liver
days.scenario:
A donor liver has become available. Two patients on the ward match it, and only one can receive it.

The first is a woman of thirty-four who has never touched alcohol. Her liver is failing from a rare inherited disease. Her doctors give her a seventy percent chance of surviving five years with the transplant.

The second is a man of fifty-one whose liver was destroyed by twenty years of drinking. He has been sober for six years, sponsors others in recovery, and has followed every instruction his doctors gave him. He has been on the list for two years. Her name was added four months ago. His five-year survival chance with the transplant is also seventy percent.

Without the organ, both will likely die within weeks. The transplant committee must decide tonight. The only difference between them is how they came to be ill, and how long they have waited.
days.question: Who should receive the liver?
days.option_a_text: The woman. Waiting time cannot outweigh the fact that his illness was self-inflicted and hers was not.
days.option_b_text: The man. Medicine treats disease, not biography, and he waited his turn.

days.title: The Well
days.scenario:
A remote village of two hundred people has one working well, dug and maintained for decades by a single family. The family has always let everyone draw water freely.

A drought has now dropped the water table. There is enough for the village to survive if strictly rationed, or enough for a small number of families to keep their livestock and gardens alive while the rest lose everything but drinking water.

The family who owns the well has proposed that they, and the four households who helped dig it a generation ago, take a larger share to save their herds, which are the only livestock in the village and the source of its milk and breeding stock. Everyone else would get drinking rations only.

The village must decide together. Some argue the water belongs equally to all who need it now, and that setting such a system up breeds a slippery slope of inequality. Others argue that without the herds, the whole village has no future once the rains return.
days.question: Should the water be split equally, or should the herd-owning families receive more?
days.option_a_text: Water is survival, and in a crisis it belongs equally to every mouth. No one's livestock outranks another's child's thirst.
days.option_b_text: Save the herds. Equal shares that leave the village with nothing to rebuild on is a fair way to starve slowly together.

days.title: The Alibi
days.scenario:
A jury is deliberating a murder charge against a nineteen-year-old named Marcus. The murder was brutal and the victim's mother underwent a nervous breakdown upon learning about what was done to her daughter. The physical evidence is thin, and the case turns almost entirely on one witness: Marcus's younger sister, Ada, who is twelve.

Ada testified, under oath, that her brother was home with her the entire night of the killing. The prosecutor has established that Marcus is the only guardian Ada has left, and that if he is convicted she will enter the care of the state. Ada told the court, weeping, "He reads to me every night. He is all I have."

The jurors know a child that age, testifying to save the person she loves and depends on, is the least reliable kind of witness. They also know that if they set her account aside, they set aside the only voice that stands between Marcus and a life sentence, and she may be telling the truth. There is no other witness to weigh her against. Her word is the whole of the doubt.
days.question: Should the jury treat Ada's testimony as credible reasonable doubt?
days.option_a_text: Believe her. A sworn account that places him elsewhere is doubt, and doubt must acquit; the state must prove its case, not the child disprove it.
days.option_b_text: Set it aside. A frightened child protecting the only family she has cannot be the reed a murder verdict rests on; that is not proof, it is love.

days.title: The Severance
days.scenario:
A small manufacturing firm is closing one of its two plants. Management has set aside a fixed pool of money for severance, enough to be meaningful but not enough to be generous to everyone.

The union representative, Maria, must recommend how to divide it. She can split it evenly, so every laid-off worker receives the same modest sum. Or she can weight it by need: larger payments to those with dependents, medical debts, or no prospect of re-employment, and far less to the young and single who will likely find work within weeks.

Many of the workers who would receive less under the needs-based plan have given the firm twenty or thirty years. They argue that severance is earned by service, not awarded by hardship, and that treating a decade of loyalty as worth the same as a single mother's rent insults everything they gave. The desperate cases argue that money should go where survival depends on it.
days.question: Should Maria divide the money evenly by service, or by need?
days.option_a_text: Severance is earned. Years of labour create a claim that hardship cannot override, and rewarding need over service betrays those who gave the most.
days.option_b_text: Money should prevent ruin. A sum that merely tops up the comfortable while others lose their homes has been misspent.

days.title: The Scholarship
days.scenario:
A university offers one fully funded scholarship each year to a student from the region's poorest district. Without it, neither finalist can afford to attend at all.

The first, Amara, has the higher grades and the stronger record by a clear margin. She is talented, hardworking, and would almost certainly succeed anywhere. Her family is poor but stable; she has a place, though unfunded, at a lesser university she could scrape through.

The second, Daniel, has weaker marks but a far harder life: no parents, part-time work since fourteen, a school that failed him at every turn. The committee believes he has more raw potential than his transcript shows, and that for him this is the only door that will ever open. If he is passed over, he will not study at all.

The scholarship exists to reward merit and to lift those the system has failed. Both cannot be honoured.
days.question: Who should receive the scholarship?
days.option_a_text: Amara. The scholarship rewards achievement, and giving it to the lesser candidate punishes the very excellence education is meant to cultivate.
days.option_b_text: Daniel. The scholarship exists to open doors that would otherwise stay shut, and Amara has one that he does not.

days.title: The Model
days.scenario:
A hospital has an AI system that reads scans for a rare, aggressive cancer. In trials it catches the cancer earlier than any human radiologist, and doctors who follow its flags save lives that would otherwise be lost.

The system was trained partly on medical images taken from patients who never consented to this use. Some of those images came from people who explicitly objected to their data being reused. The hospital board knows this. Rebuilding the system on properly consented data would take three years, and during that time patients whose cancers could have been caught early will die.

The records office has recommended the system be suspended immediately until the consent problem is resolved. The head of oncology has asked that it stay running, arguing that pulling it now means signing the death warrants of people whose scans it would have flagged next month.
days.question: Should the hospital keep using the system?
days.option_a_text: Keep it running. A tool that saves lives now cannot be switched off to honour a paperwork wrong done to others.
days.option_b_text: Suspend it. Medicine built on stolen bodies is corruption, and no life saved excuses treating people as raw material.

days.title: The List
days.scenario:
A city keeps a single waiting list for social housing. Eleven thousand households are on it, ordered by a points system built over years to be blind to charm, articulacy and connections. A family near the top has waited six years in a damp one-bedroom flat with their two children.

A woman comes to the housing office with her two children. A nine-year-old son and a four-year-old daughter. She left a violent partner eight weeks ago, has been moved between three temporary hostels, and her son has stopped speaking. A doctor writes that another move will do lasting harm. Under the points system she ranks four hundredth. A two-bedroom flat is available now, and the family on the waitlist were given hope about a change in their situation.

The officer has discretion to make an exceptional allocation. Every such allocation pushes everyone below her back, including the family of six years, who have no doctor's letter and no one to speak for them, only their place in line. It is unclear when the next flat will be available.
days.question: Should the officer give the flat to the woman and her children?
days.option_a_text: Give it to her. A rule that cannot bend for an abused and vulnerable family in front of you is not fairness, it is bookkeeping.
days.option_b_text: Follow the list. The queue is the only protection the inarticulate and unrepresented have, and to snatch away the hope they were given is wrong.

days.title: The Wrong Man's Freedom
days.scenario:
Twelve years ago a woman was killed in her home. A man named Reuben was convicted on the testimony of a single eyewitness and has served twelve years of a life sentence.

A review has now found that the eyewitness identification was obtained improperly and cannot stand. Without it there is no case, and Reuben's conviction will be quashed. He has always maintained his innocence.

The dead woman's brother has asked to speak at the hearing. He wants to say, on the record and in Reuben's presence, that he believes Reuben killed his sister, that the family has never accepted otherwise, and that they will spend the rest of their lives certain of it. He is not a witness and has no evidence. He is asking to accuse a man who is about to be declared, in law, not guilty, in the room where that happens.

The judge can permit the statement or refuse it.
days.question: Should the brother be allowed to speak?
days.option_a_text: Refuse. A man cleared by the state, even on a technicality, must not be branded a murderer on his way out of the dock by someone with no evidence.
days.option_b_text: Allow it. The family lost more than anyone here, and a court that silences their grief to protect a released man's reputation has stopped serving justice.
